the mid infrared interferometric observations of the massive young stellar objects are best explained by a powerlaw density distribution with an index of 1.0, which is consistent with the hypothesis that turbulence is the main support mechanism for massive protostellar envelopes.

1) the dust temperature in MYSOs is lower than previously thought, and 2) the dust distribution in MYSOs can be described by a simple model that includes a powerlaw density distribution, and that the powerlaw index of the envelope density is ~1.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the physical processes that determine the structure and evolution of the envelopes surrounding massive young stars.
the physical conditions in the immediate vicinity of massive young stellar object envelopes.
understanding how the environment of massive stars is structured and evolves, and the role that this plays in the formation and early evolution of massive star forming regions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
massive young stars are formed in the same manner as their low mass counterparts, but the details of the process remain to be elucidated.

the inner envelope of the BN type MYSO's in our sample is a turbulent medium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inner regions of massive star forming regions are turbulent and that the turbulent energy dissipation is the dominant heating source for the dust.
the MYSO envelopes are not spherical, but that they are best described as flattened, with the flattening axis aligned along the direction of the outflow.
the MYSO envelopes are best described by spherical geometries, with powerlaw density distributions, and with a range of powerlaw indices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the envelope of the massive star is not a simple powerlaw density distribution, and the density distribution is not a single powerlaw over the entire spatial range from 100 AU to 100 000 AU.
we can probe the innermost regions of the envelope, where the density is highest, and the envelope is still optically thick at 10 mm.

the envelope density distribution is not well described by the standard Larson-Penston density profile (index 2.0), but rather by a flatter distribution, and this has important consequences for envelope stability, and for the formation of massive stars.
